segments.narration: These scrolls turn to dust if you open them. Vesuvius carbonised an entire Roman library in 79 AD.
Workmen found them under Herculaneum in 1752. Over eighteen hundred blackened rolls, hard as coal.
Scholars sliced them open. Scraped them. Unrolled them over four years each. Most were destroyed to read a few lines. What do you do with a book that dies when you look at it?
Answer: don't open it. Researchers X-ray scanned the sealed rolls and trained software to spot ink invisible to the eye.
In 2023 a student pulled one word out of a scroll nobody had opened: porphyras, purple. By 2026 a whole scroll had been read end to end, a Stoic treatise sealed since the eruption.

verdicts.claim: Early attempts destroyed scrolls: Camillo Paderni sliced them lengthwise to copy the text, and Piaggio's unrolling machine took about four years per scroll.
verdicts.note: 90% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The Vesuvius Challenge used X-ray tomography and machine learning to read sealed scrolls without physically opening them.
verdicts.note: 71% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: In October 2023 the first word read from an unopened scroll was 'porphyras', Greek for purple, and in 2026 PHerc. 1667 became the first Herculaneum scroll virtually unwrapped and read end to end.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives October 2023 and 'porphyras' (purple) read by a 21-year-old computer science student, and the 2026 end-to-end virtual unwrapping of PHerc. 1667 recovering 22 columns of a Stoic treatise; scrollprize.org independently states PHerc. 1667 was first read end to end in 2026.
